Scheme for construction and safety of reservoirs in rural areas 
†*421. SHRI SHYAM LAL: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any scheme for the construction and safety 
of reservoirs (ponds and lakes) of rural areas in order to contain the declining 
water level; and 
(b) if so, since when and if not, reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) and (b) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
In order to contain the declining water levels, the construction and 
restoration of village ponds and other water harvesting structures, like percolation 
tanks and check dams are important activities envisaged in the three major 
Watershed Development Programmes, namely the Drought Prone Areas 
Programme (DPAP), the Desert Development Programme (DDP) and the 
Intergrated Wasteland Development Programme (IWDP) of the Department of 
Land Resources of the Ministry of Ru ral Development. Desiltation of village 
ponds and tanks is also covered under the Employment Assurance Scheme and 
the three Programmes mentioned above. In addition, the Rajiv Gandhi National 
Drinking Water Mission of the Ministry of Rural Development Provides funds 
under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and the Pradhan 
Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (Drinking Water Supply Component) for sustainability 
of sources, including rainwater harvesting. 
Activities to contain declining water levels are also taken up under the 
Watershed Development Programmes implemented by, amongst others, the 
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Environment & Forests. The Central 
Ground Water Board (of the Ministry of Water Resources) is implementing a 
Pilot Central Sector Scheme on the studies of "Ground Water Recharge" which 
has a component of rain water harvesting. Under this scheme, recharge through

several State Governments and Union Territory Administrations provide old 
age pensions from their respective Budgets.

and the funds released by the Government of India for the National Old Age

*424. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news-item captioned, "Upper- 
caste men force Dalits to leave village,"  appearing in the Hindustan Times of

(b) whether it is a fact that the Dalits are being forced to leave the 
village in Junagarh, Gujarat under threats and intimidation by Upper-caste people; 
and 
(c) if so, what action is being taken by Government to check these 
activities? 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b)on 25.06.2001, about 15 Upper-caste people threatened the Dalits of 
Khuinbadi village in Junagarh district of Gujarat to vacate the waste-land 
occupied by the Dalits. An offence was registered against them by the Vanthli 
Police Station under sections 143,506(2) of the IPC and under section 3(1 )(10) 
of the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocitie s Act, 1989. All the accused were 
asrressted and sent to judicial cust ody. Necessary police bandobast was 
maintained to protect the Dalits and their property in the village. Meanwhile, 
about 20 Dalit families sat on a fast from 26.6.2001 to 31.7.2001 in front of the 
District Collector's Office to regulari ze the waste-land occupied by them. A 
meeting was held on 31.7.2001 by the Collector Junagarh in his office in 
which the District Social Welfare Officer, local MLAs Shri Samatbhai Rathod 
and Shri Kanabhai Pulabhai and the Harijan leader of Khumbadi village were 
present. A decision was taken at the meeting that the proposal regarding 
regularization of land would be sent to the Government of Gujarat within one 
month and the sufficient police bandobast would be provided to the Harijans 
in Khumbadi village. With this assurance.the dalits concluded their fast and 
returned to Khumbadi. 
On 1.8.2001, a get-together (Sneh Milan) was arranged between the upper 
caste people and the dalits in which around 300 men, women and children from 
both the communities participated alongw ith their local leaders. Members of 
the district administration were also present on the occasion. Subsequently 
there has been no tension irvthe village. However, police bandobast and vigil 
continue in the village. 
(c) 'Public order' and 'Police' ar e State subjects as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India. The registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crimes ar e primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments. However, the Government of India has been advising the 
Staie Governments, from time to time, to give more focussed attention to 
improving administration of criminal justice system to ensure prevention of 
atrocities against Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, women and other 
vulnerable sections of the society. The advisories issued by the Government

implementation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of 
Atrocities) Act, 1989 and the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; recruitment of 
persons belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the police force; 
identification of atrocities prone areas with a view to preventing crimes, creating 
awareness among the weaker sections about their rights, etc.

[22  August,  2001] RAJYA  SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. 
VENKAIAHNAIDU): (a) and (b) To tackle fluoride and brackish 
contamination in drinking 
water, during the period 1,994-95 to 1997-98, under Sub-Mission Programme 
of ARWSP, 83 projects were sanctioned to different States at a total cost of 
about Rs. 944 crore, out of which Government of India's share is about Rs. 709 
crore. Out of these 83 projects, 20 projects are reported to have been 
completed; and  the rest are at di fferent stages of implementation. 
Rural Drinking Water Supply is a State subject. State Government implement 
rural drinking water supply schemes from their own resources. Government of 
India supplements their efforts by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Rural Drinking Water component of 
Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). As reported by the State 
Governments, as on 1.4.1999, there are 2,17,211 rural habitations are affected 
with various quality problems in the country, out of of which 36,988 habitations 
are affected with fluoride contamination, 32,597 habitations with brackishness 
and the remaining are affected with other quality problems. A fresh survey is 
presently being carried out to assess th e number of habitations affected by 
various quality problems. 
Since 1.4.1998, powers to plan, approve and implement schemes/projects 
under Sub-Mission have been delegated to the States under ARWSP. Under 
Rural Drinking Water component of PMGY, the States can also plan, approve 
and implement schemes/projects to provide safe drinking water in quality affected 
habitations, which inter alias includes habitations affected with fluoride 
contamination and brackish water.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OFHOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) to (f) After the release of Dr. 
Rajkumar from captivity by Veerappan, the State Governments of Tamil Nadu 
and Karnataka formulated a joint strategy for the purpose of nabbing Veerappan 
and requested Central Government fo r assistance of Para-Military Forces, 
weapons and equipments etc. which was provided. The two State Government 
reactivated the Special Task  Force (STF) operations assisted by the Central 
Para-Military Forces, combined onslaught of the STF and BSF compelled

Veerappan and his gang escaped into the forests leaving their personal belongings 
behind. Maran, who is the Chief of TNLA and a prominent member of Veerappan's 
gang was arrested by the STF on 15.02.2001 from a place called See thai vanam in 
the Boluvampatti reserved Forests of Coimbatore district. According to the 
State Government of Tamil Nadu, combing operations are in progress by different 
search parties of the STF constituted to nab Veerappan. 
The State Government of Tamil Nadu has requested the Central 
Government to allow retention of the BSF Battalion provided by the Central 
Government for some more time along with services of helicopters, supply of 
equipments etc. Central Government has been providing all available assistance 
as sought by the State Governments of  Karnataka and Tamil Nadu from time

the Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) envisages organisation of 
me rural poor and their training and capacity building through a process of 
social mobilisation. The group approach provides an opportunity to the rural 
poor to come together on a common platform, discuss social and economic 
issues relevant to them and arrive at collective decisions aimed at their overall 
betterment. 
At the National Conference on the 'SHG Movement in the country and 
the SGSY' held recently at the Natio nal Institute of Rural Development

restore the ecology as it is going for opencast coal mining; and 
(d) the details of steps taken in this regard during last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI 
SYED SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) MCL is exploiting coal reserves in the 
Orissa State from the underground an d opencast mines to meet the coal 
requirement of consumers situated in Or issa as well as Southern States. Coal 
reserves are being exploited by MCL economically, with deployment of suitable 
technology with due regard to safety, conservation, consumers satisfaction and 
ecology.

(c) and (d) The measures taken by MCL during the last three years are as 
under:—

backfilled which is then technically and biologically reclaimed. In 
the backfilled area planting of suitable species of trees at the rate of 
2500 Nos. per hectare is being done. 
(ii) In addition to plantation in the back-filled ground, the external 
dumps as well as the surrounding lands in the lease hold area are 
also planted with trees at the rate of 2500 Nos./hectare. 
(iii) Against diversion of forest land, "compensatory afforestation" is 
done in identified plots of the land whose title is transferred as 
forest land. 
(iv) During the last three years a total No. of 10.52 lakh trees have been 
planted. 
(v) The terminal voids in the opencast mines area are used a repositories 
of water which are used for multiple purposes e.g. meeting the 
industrial and portable water needs (after treatment) of the company 
as well as serving to recharge th e ground water table in the area. 
Thus maintaining and even improving the ecology of the 
surroundings.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The Energy Review Committee 
headed by Dr. Madhav Godbole was constituted by the Government of 
Maharashtra. The Committee has submitted its second report to the Government 
of Maharashtra on 11th July, 2001. The second report makes several 
recommendations regarding reform of the Maharashtra power sector. The 
recommendations in brief are as follows: 
* Distribution regions should not be escrowed prior to privatisation. 
* Government of Maharashtra should build consensus around its 
restructuring strategy. 
* The report of the Committee should be published for information of the 
people as soon as possible. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
* Implementation of the 'Maharashtra reform Model' evolved by the 
Committee (unbundling of Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) 
into separate generation companies, transmission company and distribution 
business). 
* Progressive privatisation of distribution. 
* Hydro generation stations and Urban plant should be corporatised as a 
single state owned entity, i.e. Maharashtra Power Corporation Ltd (MPCL). 
* Transmission and system coordination services to remain under state 
ownership.  
* Distribution companies should be configured on basis of "concentrated 
zones". This would eliminate scope of cross-subsidy. 
* Second phase of reforms should start with progressive privatisation of 
distribution companies. 
* Pre-dominant non-urban distribution companies should initially remain 
under state ownership. 
* Sale of distribution business and generating companies through 
competitive bidding. 
* Generating companies except for MPCL should progressively be privatised 
after stabilization of the distribution companies. 
* Establishment of a Power Sector Reform Fund. 
* As a preparatory step towards the establishment of a bulk market, the 
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) may consider 
regulating generation through a regulated cost-based pool, from which 
the distribution companies can source their power requirements. 
* Government of Maharashtra should take steps to vest the MERC with 
additional powers and increase its financial autonomy. 
* MERC to consider multi-year regul ation as it reduces not only the 
regulatory uncertainty but also the regulatory burden and also improves 
its quality of regulation by staggering the process of tariff application 
from different distribution companies. 
98 

[22 August,  2001] RAJYA  SABHA

listed under Section 22(2) of the Electricity Regulatory Commission's 
Act, 1998, which include regulation of investment approval and the 
operation of the power system and issuing of licenses, be entrusted to 
MERC with immediate effect. 
* MSEB to improve the information base so as to provide the MERC with a 
sufficient basis for embarking on a multi-year regulatory approach. 
* MSEB to undertake action to improve its performance to the extent possible 
(reallocation of employees, reduction of commercial payables, regularization 
of unauthorized connections). 
* Suitable laws to be enacted to give MSEB/Government of Maharashtra 
powers to penalize the guilty. MSEB to get a study commissioned to

6000 crores from Rs. 200 crores during the period of 30 years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) With the object of minimizing cost and time 
overruns of Hydro-electric Projects, Government has introduced from June, 
2001, a policy of 3-stage development of new Central sector Hydro-electric 
Projects. Under Stage-I, activities leading to formulation of pre-feasibility 
report for assessment of commercial viability of the Project are envisaged. 
Stage-II relates to preparation of detailed project report, acquisition of land 
for project construction area, obtaini ng of requisite clearances and pre-
construction activities including infrastructure. Actual construction of the 
project is envisaged in Stage-Ill.

(b) In 1972, Tehri Dam Project (600MW) was initially approved as a State 
Sector Project to be implemented by Government of U.P. at an estimated cost of 
Rs. 197.92 crores. The capacity of the Project was enhanced to 1000 MW in 1983. 
However, in view of the resource constraints faced by the State Government and 
keeping in view the requirement of power in the Northern Region of the country, 
it was decided in November, 1986 to implement the Tehri Dam Complex comprising 
(i) Tehri Dam and Hydro Electric Project (HEP) Stage-I (1000 MW), (ii) Koteshwar 
Dam and Power Project (400 MW) and (iii) Tehri Pump Storage Plan (PSP) (1000 
MW) as a joint venture of Government of India and the Government of Uttar 
Pradesh. These projects are being executed through the Tehri Hydro Development 
Corporation (THDC). 
In March, 1994, approval was accorded to the Tehri Hydro Development 
Corporation for implementing the Tehri Dam and HEP Stage-I (1000 MW) at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 3391.40 (March, 1993 Price Level) including IDC of Rs. 
427.74 crores. The cost estimates included the committed works of Koteshwar 
HEP and essential works of Tehri PSP. 
The revised cost estimates of the Tehri HEP Stage-I (1000 MW) including 
essential works of Tehri PSP are Rs. 5690.64 Crores (August 1999 Price Level) 
including IDC and financial charges. The increase in the cost, apart from normal 
escalation, has been due to various factors including design changes to ensure 
safety of the Dam in the context of the seismicity of the region, additional measures 
for rehabilitation of project affected families based on the recommendations of 
Hanumantha Rao Committees, availing of specialized consultancy services, foreign 
exchange variation and variation in statutory duties and levies, etc.

3270. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any accident took place in the NTPC Cooling Tower Project 
under construction at Vishakhapatnam during the last week of March, 2001. 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any enquiries have been c onducted into the causes of the 
accident and responsibilities fixed therefor; 
100 

[22  August,  2001] RAJYA  SABHA 
(d) if so, the details thereof;

died or were injured as a result of the accident; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) An accident took place in Cooling Tower No. 
1 at Simhadri Thermal Power Project of the National Thermal Power Corporation 
(NTPC) on 28th March, 2001. The construction work of Cooling Tower is being 
executed by M/s National Building Construction Corporation (NBCC), a 
Government of India Undertaking, under a turnkey contract. The temporary access 
to facilitate transport of material was made of scaffolding pipes to the height of 165 
meters. This temporary access scaffolding collapsed at about 10.30 PM on 28th 
March, 2001 due to which six persons of sub-contractor of M/s NBCC succumbed 
to injuries and one person who was admitted to hospital was discharged on 
6.62001. 
(c) and (d) A high level Enquiry Committee had been constituted by 
NTPC to enquire into the accident. The Committee submitted its report. The 
Committee feels that the cumulative f actors like accidental jamming of the 
concrete bucket with the structure resulting in loosening of some couplers 
and loss of some members, possible loosening of some of the couplers of the 
scaffolding contributed to the accident and that the responsibility lies with 
M/s NBCC. The Committee suggested various recommendations to M/s NBCC 
to prevent recurrence of similar accident. 
(e) and (0 An ex-gratia of Rs. 2.50 lakh to each family of those killed in the 
accident has been paid by M/s NBCC. Besides, statutory payment of about Rs. 
2.00 lakh as compensation under Workmen's Compensation Act is also being 
paid. Further, the treatment charges of the injured person as well as salary for 
that period has been paid by M/s NBCC.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The tariffs for NTPC power stations upto 
May, 1999 were determined by Govt, of India as per provisions in the Electricity 
(Supply) Act, 1948. Thereafter this function now vests with Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (CERC) as per the provision in the Electricity 
Regulatory Commission Act, 1998. They have determined a few provisional 
tariffs for newly commissioned units. The CERC have decided that tariffs so

and in accordance with the Regional Energy Accounts issued by Regional 
Electricity Boards. Therefore, NTPC ha s not overcharged the states for the 
power sold by them. 
(c) Pursuant to a decision taken in the Chief Minister's conference in 
March, 2001, the Expert Committee constituted by Government of India under 
the Chairmanship of Member (Energy), Planning Commission has submitted 
its report on one time settlement of outstanding dues of SEBs payable to 
CPSUs on 11.5.2001. The Expert Group has recommended substantial incentive 
to the State utilities to settle past dues and ensure full payment in future. 
These benefits include: 
(i)     Partial write-off of surcharge to the extent of 50% thereof. 
(ii)     CPSUs to give 2% of bond amount as cash incentive to those SEBs 
who open and maintain LCs without default by the specified dates. 
(iii)     Issuance of the tax-free bonds by the State Govts. 
(iv)    The cash incentives for a period of 4 year @4% of the face value of the 
bonds to SEBs for achieving the prescribed performance milestones by the 
SEBs. Recommendations of the Expert Group were considered by the High 
Level Empowered Group of Chief Ministers and these Recommendations have 
been accepted with the following modifications, (a)    The Waiver of

Waiving off additional comfort and security from BPP 
3275. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh has very recently urged 
Union Power Minister to have conditions of additional comfort and security 
being insisted upon by financial institutions from independent producers waived 
as reported in 'The Hindu" (Delhi Edition) dated the 8th April, 2001; 
(b) if so, details thereof and reasons for waiving the conditions; 
(c) whether a meeting of financial institutions have since been held to 
consider the matter and making n ecessary changes in Memoranda of 
Understanding/Agreement; and 
(d) if so, the details of decision taken by financial institutions in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to  (d) With a view to identify an acceptable 
payment security mechanism for Independent Power Producers (IPPs), in the 
eighth meeting of the Crisis Resolution Group (CRF) held on March 30, 
2000 under the chairmanship of Minister of Power, various alternatives to 
escrow were discussed. In this meeting, it was decided that financing of IPPs 
should be linked with the progress of reforms undertaken by the State 
Government. To facilitate private power projects to achieve financial closure, 
the Ministry of Power has proposed a reform based security mechanism as an 
alternative to escrow to provide financial comfort to the lenders and IPP 
promoters. The Financial Institutions have agreed to undertake financing of 
IPPs on the basis of a legally binding agreement to be made by State 
Governments to provide escrow before commercial Operation Date instead 
of the present practice of escrow at the time of financial closure. In pursuance 
of this decision, a draft Memorandum  of Agreement (MoA) was prepared. 
After several rounds of discussions between the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh/APTRANSCO and the Indian Financial Institutions/Banks, the MoA, 
which ensures financing of 6 private power projects in Andhra Pradesh with 
a total capacity of 2239 MW, has been initialed by the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh/APTRANSCO, Power Finance Corporation and the Financial 
Institutions led by Industrial Development Bank of India on August, 10,2001. 
Under the proposed MoA, APTRANSCO would be able to open escrow 
account 30 days before Commercial Operation Date instead of the present 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
requirement of escrow before financial closure. During the interim period, the 
APTRANSCO would provide a charge on its receivables to the Financial 
Institutions.

3280. SHRI BJ. PANDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state:

improving the overall PLF in the State Sector to a minimum of 65 per cent and

all new electricity connections to agriculture sector exceeding 10 H.P. by 2002 
A.D.;

Tackling drinking water problem in Kerala 
3287. SHRI CO. POULOSE. W ill the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news-item captioned "Wells do a 
vanishing trick in Kerala" appearing in the Hindu dated 23rd June, 2001; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
(b) whether wells which are the main source of drinking water for rural 
people in the State, have caved and cease to exist; 
(c) if so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what action is being taken by Government in tackling the drinking 
water problem of the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As per the records available with the Central Ground Water Board, 
about 140 wells have caved in the season (June-July, 2001), collapsed partially 
or completely in difference districts of Kerala State. 
(c) As per the findings of the Committee consisting of Central Ground 
Water Board, Centre for Earth Sciene Studies, Mines and Geology and the 
Geological Survey of India, the main r easons that appear to have contributed 
to the wells collapse are the type of well lining, lithological conditions, rainfall 
intensity and recharge, and absence of free flow of water across the well lining 
from the aquifer to the well. The sudden build up of different water pressure 
has also been attributed as another reason to the incidents of wells collapse. 
(d) Drinking water supply being a State subject, schemes for providing 
drinking water facilities to rural habitations are implemented by the States 
from their own resources. The Government of India supplements the efforts of 
the States by providing financial assistance under the Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Rural Drinking Water component of the 
Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). The wells which are reported 
to have caved in or collapsed in different districts in Kerala State are private 
wells and do not come under the rural drinking water supply schemes 
implemented by the Government. 
Kerala Government has been allocated Rs. 63.31 crore under ARWSP 
and Rs. 7.74 crore under Rural Drinking Water component of PMGY for the 
current year, out of which Government of India have already released Rs. 31.65 
crore as first instalment under ARWSP.

Acute problem of potable drinking water in Saurashtra 
3294. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the whole of Saurashtra is facing an acute 
problem of potable drinking water for the third consecutive year; 
(b) if so, what immediate steps are being taken in this regard; and 
(c) what measures are being taken to solve the problem on a permanent 
basis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) As reported by 
the Government of Gujarat, Saurashtra Region of the State was under the grip 
of acute shortage of water for two consecutive years, i.e. 1999-2000 and 
2000-2001. During the current monsoo n, the State has been receiving 
satisfactory rainfall. The pr esent storage in Saurashtra Reservoirs is 36% of 
the designed capacity and as the current monsoon is still on, it is expected 
that these reservoirs will be further replenished. However, reservoir supplying 
water to cities like Jamnagar and Rajkot, as on date, are not adequately 
replenished and need more inflow of water to sustain supplies to these up to 
next monsoon. 
(b) and (c) As reported by the Government of Gujarat, the State 
Government has implemented a bulk water pipeline project for transfer of Mahi/ 
Narmada water from Central and South Gujarat to Saurashtra for meeting the 
needs of drinking water supply to the districts of Amreli, Bhavnagar, parts of 
Rajkot and Junagadh. Towns and cities in Saurashtra region have been 
supplied water during the scarcity period. Drinking water works relating to 
distribution network are going on in Bhavnagar and Amreli districts at a total 
cost of Rs. 450 crore. Government of Gujarat has also sanctioned a project at 
an estimated cost of Rs. 1106 crore for supplying Narmada water drawn from 
Maliya Branch to the districts of Ja mnagar and Kachchh. The project is 
planned to be completed by December, 2002. These projects are part of the 
major drinking water supply projects based on the Sardar Sarovar Canal as 
source to cover 8215 villages and 195 towns of Saurashatra and Kachchh.

Acute shortage of drinking water in Himachal Pradesh 
3298. SHRIMATI CHANDRESH KUMARI: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether acute shortage of safe drinking water in Himachal Pradesh has 
been reported to Government; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the situation has become worse in Himachal Pradesh after 
sever drought like situation developed in the absence of sufficient rain-falls 
and snow-fall during last winter season; 
 
(d) whether Government were requested to provide special Central 
assistance to Himachal Pradesh to enable the State Government to undertake 
various projects to augment drinking water supply in rural areas of Himachal 
Pradesh; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) As reported by 
the Government of Himachal Pradesh, due to insufficient snowfall during the 
last two winters and scanty winter rains, there has been considerable reduction 
in the discharge of various water sources which are otherwise perennial in nature. 
The State experienced less than normal rainfall during the period between 1-1-
2001 to 28-2-2001 and this situation has led to drought like condition in the State. 
(d) The State Government has submitted a Memorandum to the Government 
of India requesting for an emergent relief of Rs. 90.25 crore including Rs. 32.40 
crore for drinking water supply relief measures. 
(e) The primary responsibility for dealing with natural calamity including 
drought rests with the State Government. The main source of financing relief 
expenditure is the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) for which 75% share is contributed 
by the Central Government. For major calamities, where funds in the CRF do not 
suffice, assistance is admissible from the National Calamity Contingency Fund 
(NCCF). These arrangements are in accordance with the award of the Eleventh 
Finance Commission (EFC). Apart from releasing the entire Central share of CRF

for 2001 -2002 amounting to Rs. 34.24 crore, a special assistance of Rs. 18.98 crore 
has also been released from the NCCF for drought to Government of Himachal 
Pradesh.

subject. Government of India supplements the efforts of the State by providing 
financial assistance under the Acceler ated Rural Water Supply Programme 
(ARWSP) and Rural Drinking Water component of Prime Minister's Gramodaya 
Yojana (PMGY). During 2000-2001, Rs. 53.85 crores under ARWSP and Rs. 
30.77 crores under Rural Drinking Water component of PMGY have been 
released to State Government. During the current financial year i.e. 2001-2002, 
an allocation of Rs. 55.59 crore has been made under ARWSP including DDP 
areas out of which Rs. 27.76 crore have been released and under Rural Drinking 
Water component of PMGY, Rs. 7.91 crore have been allocated out of which 
Rs. 3.95 crore have been releasd to the Government of Himachal Pradesh. 
Further to facilitate the mitigation efforts, in view of the prevailing 
scarcity of drinking water in rural ar eas of Himachal Pradesh on account of 
drought, the priorities fixed in the ARWSP guidelines have ben relaxed by 
the Government of India to the extent that the funds under ARWSP and Rural 
Drinking Water component of PMGY could also be utilised for activities 
relating to repair, rejuvenation, renov ation, restoration and replacement of 
existing rural drinking water schemes in areas affected by scarcity of drinking 
water in the State.

Earnings from Taj Mahal and amount spent for its Maintenance 
†3352. SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK: Will the Minister of TOURISM 
AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the annual earning of the Government from Taj Mahal and annual amount 
spent for its maintenance; 
(b) the reasons behind handing over the Taj Mahal to private sector; 
(c) whether Government would regain its control of Taj Mahal by repealing its 
order; and 
(d) if so, by when and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) During the year 2000-2001 an amount of Rs. 8.48 crores has been 
collected and deposited in the consolidated fund of the Government of India and 
an expenditure of Rs. 21.00 lakhs has been incurred for its structural repairs and 
annual maintenance. 
(b) to (d) The Taj Mahal has not been handed over to the private sector, but 
under the aegis of the National Culture Fund, the Archaeological Survey of India 
have signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Indian Hotel Company Ltd. 
to provide financial assistance towards conservation, environmental development and 
improvement of tourist related facilities. All conservation measures identified under the 
Memorandum of Understanding will be carried out by the Archaeological Survey 
of India alone.

Agriculture Crops Insurance Scheme 
SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to raise the matter 
regarding assessment of loss or damage to standing crops during natural 
calamities like floods and drought. Under the present Crop Insurance Scheme, 
"Harvest Tests' for assessing the loss or  damage to crops are being made by 
one or two survey members of one or two villages in a Taluk. They take the 
earlier year's production into considera tion. The difference in production of 
the previous year and the year in wh ich the crops are affected by natural 
calamities, is assessed. Accordingly,  compensation is paid to farmers. 
Because of this practice adopted for pu rposes of the Crop Insurance Scheme, 
farmers are unable to get the exact compensation for their loss. This method 
of loss assessment is not beneficial to farmers in getting compensation. The 
"Harvest Test' should be done by insurance people in all the villages which 
are affected by natural calamities, or, in, at least, fifty per cent of the affected 
villages so that the actual loss to farmers comes to light. Thereafter, an 
average of the loss or damage may be taken into consideration for purposes of 
compensation. 
I, therefore, request the Government to take necessary action for 
making suitable modifications in the existing method of assessment of loss or 
damage to crops in order to help farmers in getting a reasonable 
compensation.

GOVERNMENT BILLS 
THE MARRIAGE LAWS (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominat ed): Sir, I rise to support 
the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2001. It is a matter of great shame that 
54 years after Independence, the women in our country face severe 
discrimination since their birth. In fact, they are not even allowed to be bom. 
The latest Census figures indicate that, in the age group of 0-6, the 
200 
 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
 
number of girls is less, compared to the boys. Alarmingly, it has gone down. 
It should be a matter of concern to all right-minded individuals. Girls are 
discriminated against and they are also denied equal access to food, nutrition, 
health, education and em ployment. Consequently, they end up by being 
totally dependent on either their father or their brother and later on their 
husbands. Alongwith this, the mind-set that exists is, the parents think that 
their primary duty -- in fact, their only duty- towards their daughter is to get 
her married off and then wash their hands off.   
यह माना जाता है िक िजस घर मȂ 
लड़की की डोली जाती है उस घर से िसफर्  उसकी अथीर् वापस आनी चािहए । Alongwith 
this, the constant pressure from all sections of the society to keep the 
marriage alive, under all circumstances , makes it almost impossible for the 
girl to leave an abusive home. There have been instances when a girl has 
gone back to her parents and has said, "my husband beats me", and the 
parents instead of saying, "this should not be allowed" have actually said 
"पित ही तो है , एकाध थÃपड़ मार िदया तो क्या" and sent her back to that abusive 
home. Such is the situation; which is why the women have to tolerate the 
abusive relations in our society. Sir, filing for divorce is an almost impossible 
exercise, because, firstly, it is a trauma tising experience, and, secondly, there 
is a great drain on the financial resources. She has absolutely no State 
support. If she goes back to her parents' home, she seriously jeopardises the 
chances of her younger sister getting married. She has no income of her own. 
And, so, it becomes an almost impossible exercise. 
Under these circumstances, one welcomes the Marriage Laws 
(Amendment) Bill, 2001. But, Sir, on cl osest scrutiny, one finds that the Bill 
seems to have a singular objective of introducing a 'time cap of 60 days' from 
the date of receipt of notice, on interim applicants for: 
 Alimony and expenses or litigation (Section 36 of the Indian Divorce 
Act, 1869). 
 Expenses on the suit, weekly or monthly pendente life maintenance 
(Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Section 49 of the Parsi 
Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936; and Section 36 of the Special Marriage 
Act, 1954). 
 Maintenance and education of children (Section 26 of the Hindu 
Marriage Act, 1955; Section 39 of th e Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 
1936; and Section 38 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954). 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
Now, often, these applications fail on account of the term 'income' 
of the husband being vaguely defined. Very often, the husbands pass of their 
life-style maintenance on to the comp any. That is why it is extremely 
important that the law should enable the Court to make sure that the lifestyle 
of the husband is also included; never mind if he pays for it or his company 
pays for it.   Therefore, the following amendment is suggested: 
"Provided that any application shall not be determined merely on the 
basis of income tax returns or any statement produced by the 
respondent. The court shall take into account the life-style of the 
respondent as evident from his expenditure on food, clothing, 
entertainment, housing, personal items and travel, irrespective of 
whether such expenditure is incurred or borne by the respondent in 
person or incurred or borne by any other person or company." 
Then, there should also be an easy way of recovering the amount of 
maintenance that is ordered. Accordingly, the law should empower the court 
to direct the employer to deduct from the husband's salary and pay directly to 
the wife. And, a similar provision may also be made in the case of debtors. 
The following amendment is accordingly suggested : 
"Where the Court is of the opinion that it is in the interest of justice, 
notwithstanding anything in any law in force, it may, by an order, 
direct the employer of the respondent or his debtor, to deduct the 
amount of monthly allowance of maintenance or expenses payable 
from his salary or debt and to directly pay the same to applicant." 
Sir, often, it becomes difficult to get the Respondent to disclose his 
assets. Also, often, the woman has to continue with the litigation without any 
money. Therefore, it is suggested that the Respondent be compelled to make a 
disclosure of assets, and make self-assessment of his liability (for a period of 
sixty days, i.e., until the interim appli cation can be decided), which amount 
has to be deposited with the court for disbursal to the applicant. The 
following amendment is suggested : 
"A person receiving notice of such an application shall be required to 
submit a self-assessment of his means and a computation of what 
would be his liability as maintenance expenses payable for a period 
of sixty days along with his reply to the Magistrate and shall deposit 
with the Magistrate the amount so computed for disbursal to the 
applicant.   An allowance under this section shall be payable 
202 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
from the date of the order, or, if so ordered, from the date of the 
application." 
Sir, along with it, Section 25(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act 
stipulates that maintaining "chastity" is essential to continue to enjoy the 
right to maintenance. This provision is moralistic and archaic and is often 
used to harass and embarrass lady litigants. It is recommended that this 
provision be deleted. 
Now, Sir, Section 27 of the Hind u Marriage Act enables the Court 
to make provisions for the disposal of joint property. However, property 
acquired during the subsistence of the ma rriage, in the name of either spouse 
and all household goods acquired during the marriage, are not covered by 
this section. This section should be amended to enable the court to allocate 
all such property in an equitable manner to either party, on the dissolution of 
the marriage. This will enable the court to take into consideration the

THE ADVOCATES' WELFARE FUND BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
AND THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam, I 
move:- 
"That the Bill to provide for the constitution of a welfare 
fund for the benefit of advo cates and for mattersconnected 
therewith or incidental thereto, as passed by the Lok Sabha, 
be taken into consideration*. 
Madam, I will just explain the need for a Bill of this kind and what 
the salient features of this Bill are. It had been a longstanding demand of the 
lawyers all over the country that a Central legislation of this kind should be 
drafted. There are several State G overnments and State Assemblies which 
have already a law of this kind in pl ace and we had different experiences of a 
law of that kind. This law protects each one of them, unless those State 
Assemblies or the State Governments decide that they may find this as a 
beneficial provision and decide to transf er themselves and their lawyers into 
the benefits of this Bill. 
The scheme of this Bill is that it bears in mind that professionals 
otherwise do not have any element of social security. There is i .0 Provident 
Fund. There is no gratuity. There is no pension. Some of them, of course, do 
earn very well. But the earnings of a very large number of them are not so 
high as to even sustain them or their families out of the savings that they have. 
This Bill, under section 3, cons titutes an Advocates' Welfare Fund. 
There are enabling clauses as to fr om where monies can come in. The 
Governments can also make contributions to the Fund. 
214 

[22 August. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The Bar Councils, the Bar Associations, can make contributions to 
the Funds, but the principal distinction between this and the State Funds is -- 
we have studied the experience of all the States -- we had written to all the 
States to share those experiences with us -- I also had a occasion to discuss it 
with the cross-section of the la wyer community an d their elected 
representatives — one of the problems that we noted was — that membership 
in a large number of State Funds was no t compulsory, and, therefore, when it 
was made optional, the optional memb ership experience did not succeed in 
some States. It succeeded where the me mbership was compulsory. So. -there 
is a compulsory membership; there is an  entry fee into the Fund; there is an 
annual renewal fee. The principal source of funding, in addition to this, comes 
from two sources. Twenty per cent of what the Bar Councils collect, by way 
of enrolment fee from lawyers, will be transferred to this Fund. And, 
additionally, every lawyer -- it has been made clear in this Bill -- out of his 
own earning, and not by transferring the burden to his clients, is expected to 
put a welfare stamp on the wakalatnama of every case he files. Now, this 
welfare stamp, for subordinate courts, has been fixed at five rupees; for 
tribunals, other authorities, High Courts, Supreme Courts, it has been kept at 
ten rupees. So, there are two sides in a case, the amount will get doubled 
because both will have to put that welfare stamp. This Welfare Fund would 
be managed and administered by a committee which is constituted in every 
State. The Committee would be headed by the Advocate General of .the State. 
It will have the Chairman of the Bar Council, Secretary of the Bar Council, 
the Law Secretary of the State Govern ment and also some members of the 
Bar Council. It is this Committee which will administer this Fund. The sale of 
these stamps will also be administered  by this Committee. There are several 
terms with regard 10 the appointment of members and their disqualifications, 
but section 18 makes the membership of the Fund compulsory for all 
advocates. 
With regard to the benefits that the advocates would get out of this 
Fund, there are three different provisions. Section 19, section 21 and section 
24. Section 19 provides for a Trust, giving an ex-gratia payment to any 
member of the Fund, in the event of his serious illness or surgery -- they will 
take into consideration all circumstances; what his other financial 
circumstances are. Section 21 has a Schedule attached to the Bill, that on 
cessation of practice, a token amount w ill be given to every advocate. The 
third and the most important section is section 24 which provides for different 
kinds of assistances which can be given,  like obtaining group 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
insurances, life insurances, medical and educational facilities, for young 
lawyers, some assistance in terms of books. And there are other provisions 
which can be made, in the event of his d. th. Whatever scheme the State 
Committee, the Trust Committee, would fo n.jlate, his family members would 
get that assistance, in the event of his death, and this amount will actually be a 
substantial amount. In the even of his death, it will be the social security 
amount which is given to his family. There is also a provision, that because 
amenities in various courts are still lacking, 10 per cent of what is collected 
will be spent on common amenities, as far as the district and the subordinate 
Bar Associations are concerned, because that is where the amenities are 
required to be improved upon. 
There are two other provisions. One, some of the benefits of this 
Fund may not be available to those who are designated senior advocates 
because it is presumed that they have a larger practice, and, therefore, may 
not need the benefits of this Fund  -- they are only entitled to certain 
collective group benefits out of this Fund. There is also a provision that as 
far as the Schedules attached to this  Fund are concerned, if some States 
have a larger amount available with them, they can always amend and 
improve upon those Schedules, in the cont ext of those States. There is also 
an appeal provision; if somebody is dissatisfied with any decision of the 
Trust which has been created, an appeal  lies to the full Bar Council of that 
particular State. Theref ore, the overall scheme, as far as this Bill is 
concerned, appears to be that, substantially, the funds for this will come 
from the legal community themselves, unless somebody voluntarily gives to 
them. These funds would be administered and improved upon by depositing 
them or by group insurance, etc. There would be a Committee comprising 
of their own elected representatives, w ith the Advocate Gene ral as the head, 
which would provide the social secur ity mechanism. Now, I must mention 
that 16 States -- this is specified in Schedule II -- have already legislated. 
We have included a saving clause in re spect of all these State legislations 
because the subject is in the Concu rrent List. Unless, on account of 
compulsory membership and certain othe r salient features, some States feel 
that it is beneficial to come within the scope of the Central legislation, then
  
we have the power to delete that particular State out of Schedule II, and they 
would also be entitled to the benefits of the Central legislation. Madam, I 
propose that this House takes this up for consideration and approval. 
The question was proposed.

SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam. I rise to support the Advocates ' Welfare Fund Bill , 2001. The object 
of the Bill, that is, to provide social security to advocates, is laudable. The 
advocates play a vital rote in protecting the rights of the citizens and also in 
upholding the rule of law. Madam, the role played by the lawyers during the 
freedom struggle is commendable; ther efore, any move to create a welfare 
fund for the lawyers must be supported. Sir, while supporting the Bill, I would 
like to point out one or two things. The Bill proposes to bring about 
uniformity in the operation of Advocates' Welfare Fund in various States. But 
Madam, the purpose of the Bill is virtually watered down by the saving 
clause. As per this clause, this Act will not apply to the 16 States which have 
their own laws, as specified in Schedule II. Therefore, there is a possibility of 
these 16 States not adopting this Bill when it becomes an Act. Sir, it will be 
better if, in a matter like this, there is some uniformity throughout the country. 
Now, Madam, I would like to point out the second anomaly. The 
Bill provides that whenever the Committee is superseded, the funds are

transferred to the appropriate Governme nt. There is also a provision in the 
Bill that the Committee has to be re-constituted within a period of six 
months. If that is the case, why sh ould the funds be transferred to the 
Government? I feel, it is wholly unnecessary, and this can be deleted. 
Sir, the other thing that I would like to suggest, which I feel is very, 
very important, is that the interest of the young advocates, the advocates who 
enrol themselves, has to be protected. Ju st as we are taking care of advocates 
who have given up practice, who are old in age. similarly, the young lawyers 
need to be supported. Madam, it is at th at time they require a lot of support, 
as they go through a lot of priva tions and difficulties. Therefore, my 
suggestion is that some amount must be earmarked for the welfare of the 
young advocates, particular ly, for enabling them to set up libraries, because 
library is a tool for any advocate. Some portion of the financial assistance 
must be earmarked for this purpose. 
Madam, another important thing, I feel, is that there should not be 
any fetters on the Committee as to who should be given the benefits and who 
should not, because the Committee is headed by the Advocate-General, and 
competent Advocates are there on the Co mmittee. Therefore, it must be left 
to the discretion of the Committee to decide as to who should get the benefit. 
The best beneficiaries should be thos e who need the fund the most.  I am 
borrowing the words of the hon. Minister. 
Madam, the last point that I would like to make is that it would have 
been ideal had the Central Government given some corpus to the Advocates' 
Welfare Fund. Their concern for the we lfare of the advocates would have 
been better appreciated had they contributed some amount to it. I understand, 
some States are doing this. If the Central Government also thinks on those 
lines, it would be better, but, anyway, there is a provision which says that the 
Central and State Governments can contribute money to this welfare fund. 
With these words. Madam, I support the Bill. Thank you.

Failure of Public Distribution System and

SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to participate in 
the discussion on the failure of the public distribution system and the need for 
revamping it. Sir, I think, this issue is of serious concern to one and all, 
irrespective of political affiliations. Therefore, I feel, this issue should be kept 
above politics. This is my humble submission. 
Sir, two days back, the Supreme Court had expressed a serious 
concern over the starvation deaths in some States and observed, "It is the 
primary responsibility of the Central Government and State Governments to 
ensure the foodgrains overflowing in the FCI godowns reach ed the starving 
people and not wasted by dumping them in the sea or eaten by rats." It has 
further observed, "Even if the foodgrains had to be given free, it should be 
done as no person should be deprived  of food, merely because he had no 
money." Even the Planning Commission, in its mid-term appraisal of the 
Ninth Five-Year Plan has mentioned, "All is not well with the PDS." The 
subsidy earmarked for the PDS in 1997-98 was of Rs.7,500 crores. Now it 
has gone up to Rs. 12.042 crores. Much  of this subsidy is not reaching the 
families living below the poverty line for whom it is earmarked. 
Sir, in response to several complaints and recommendations of the 
Standing Committee, a study was conducted by the Tata Economic 
Consultancy Services. It was found that 36 per cent of wheat, 31 per cent of 
rice, and 23 per cent of sugar was diverted. The diversion is more in the 
Northern States, Eastern States and in the North-Eastern Region. I am quoting 
this from the mid-term appraisal document. It is comparatively less in the  
Southern and Western regions. 
A high 64 per cent diversion of rice is estimated in Bihar and Assam. 
The hon. Minister, while replying to the debate on the FCI Bill, stated that a 
quantity of 303 lakh tonnes has been allotted to the States and UTs, but they 
have lifted only 130 lakh tonnes. Even at the ration shop level, the offtake is less. 
The reasons for the poor offtake at the ration shop level can be only two. One is 
the lack of purchasing power and the other is the bad quality of foodgrains. 
266 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
It has been said in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Plan that 
some of the problems associated with the scheme are - 
1. The poor do not have cash to buy 20 kg at a time and often they are 
not permitted to buy in instalments; 
2. Low quality of foodgrains. A Worl d Bank report (June, 2000) states 
that half of the Food Corporation's grains stocks is at least two years 
old; 30 per cent, between 2 to 4 years old; and some grains, as old as 
16 years. 
3. Price charged exceeds the official pr ice by 10 to 14 per cent at the 
ration shop level. 
The Planning Commission also attributed that the lack of land 
reforms and failure of poverty alleviation programmes is also a reason for the 
lack of purchasing power. The Hon. Mi nister blames the States for not 
reaching the foodgrains to the needy poor and stated  that the distribution 
system is not proper. I need not dispute the statement of the hon. Minister. 
But I humbly submit that the Centre also bears an equal responsibility in 
implementing the Public Distribution System effectively. The Centre simply 
cannot wash off its hands by allotting foograins to the States. The Centre 
should study how some States could implement the Public Distribution 
System effectively, whose offtake from the FCI and at the ration shop level is 
almost 100 per cent and how some States  are unable to lift the stocks and 
distribute to the needy poor. The hon. Food Minister should have discussions 
and consultations with the State Governments about the problems and 
hurdles, if any, being faced in the implementation and find a methodology for 
an effective implementation of the Public Distribution System at the root 
level. 
Of ail the issues before the nation, I feel, PDS is the issue of utmost 
concern. Hence I appeal to the Prime Mini ster to give the utmost priority and 
take all the necessary steps for revamping the Public Distribution System at 
the earliest. The role of political and social workers and public 
representatives at the village level is very important and crucial in the 
implementation of the Public Distribution System. I am sorry to say that most 
of our village level workers are not evincing a keen interest in this 
programme. I appeal to the political and social workers at the village level to 
take utmost interest in the proper functioning of the Public Distribution 
System.

MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, the food sector of 
the country is in a mess right now. It is completely created by the present

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I 
must express my anguish at the very outset that in real terms, the sad demise 
of the Public Distribution System has already taken place and the present 
Government is only busy in performing the funeral rites of the PDS so that 
any future discussion about this issue can be put to rest. I remember the diktat 
of the international money lending organisations, when they advised the 
Government of India, way back in mid eighties or early eighties -- which was 
pronounced on the floor of the Parliament by an opposition Member --the 
diktat was "Thou shalt have to reduce subsidies on the food items of mass 
consumption, even if it is painful." I add, even if it leads to starvation deaths 
of the common people of the country. I am sorry to make my observation that 
the people who held power in this country in hitherto Governments hardly 
cared for the poor, the ma rginalised, ill-fated, people. For them, only some 
lip-service and electoral assurances we re considered to be sufficient. 
However, let me come back to one of th e most bizarre features of the present 
PDS, virtually, we are discussing a post-facto situation, making a post-facto 
analysis of the present system. It is quite intriguing that contrary to the 
predicament, as I have already stated , suddenly, the food subsidy has been 
increased by almost 50'per cent. But has the PDS distributed 50 per cent more 
grains? No. I want to say that the foodgrain offtake from PDS has 
plummeted. In 1999-2000, the offtake of wheat was less than half the 
allocation. In the first nine months of 2000-2001, the offtake was a little over 
one-third of the allocation. In the case of rice, in 1999-2000, the offtake was 
4/5th of the allocation. In the first nine months of 2000-2001. The offtake fell 
to a little over half the allocation. During 1998-2001 there was a boom in the 
procurement of both rice and wheat. So , the procurement continued and the 
offtake plummetted. It is a paradoxical situation. The foodgrains stock rose to 
a staggering proportion, much above the buffer stock norms. Thereby a 
disastrous situation arose. I want to give some instances as to how the issue 
prices of wheat and rice under the PDS have gone up. Let me quote some 
figures, the rate per 
285 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
quintal. In 1999-2000, the rate of the so-called BPL wheat, per quintal was 
Rs.250, whereas in 2000-2001, it is Rs.415, a rise of 66 per cent. In the APL 
cases, in 1999-2000, it was Rs.682; and in 2000-2001, it is Rs.830, a 
stagerring rise of 21.7 per cent. In the case of rice, it is from Rs.352 to 
Rs.565, that is, a 61.4 per cent rise in  the issue price; and from Rs.905 to 
Rs.1130, that is, a 24.9 per cent rise in the issue price. Whom have we 
benefited? Let us understand that. The reason for that is, perhaps, known to 
all. and that is, the steep rise in the issue prices of foodgrains under the Public 
Distribution System has cut the pff-take, leading to huge idle stocks and 
higher operating costs. The so-called APL consumers have been virtually 
evicted from the arena of the PDS by pricing foodgrains at the FCI's so-called 
'economic cost' which is near the market price in most of India and even 
higher in some places of the country. The hon. Mini ster of Food and Civil 
Supplies must note this. Naturally, the APL consumers had to opt out of the 
PDS en masse. That leaves only the BPL cons umers, the below poverty line 
consumers, who are to receive grains at fifty per cent of the economic cost. In 
many States, the Governments have managed to whittle down the number of 
BPL consumers to a fraction of the official poverty estimates. 
The 2000-01 Budget announced that  the allocation per BPL family 
had been increased from 10 kg. a month to 20 kg. If the entire BPL allocation 
had been drawn in the course of the year, the off-take would have been 14.3 
million tonnes, which would have required a subsidy of Rs.7500 crores. 
However, it appeared that in fact, even  the BPL allocation had not been fully 
drawn, since, during the first nine months of the year, less than 8.5 million 
tonnes were drawn. On an extended calculation for 12 months, it could be at 
best it.3 million tonnes. Of this, the subsidy would be around Rs.6000 crores, 
even assuming that virtually all the off-take is BPL. As against less than 
Rs.6000 crores of actual subsidy, the food subsidy was Rs. 12,215 crores. 
That is, more than half the so-called food subsidy was spent as carrying cost 
of the swelling foodgrains stock. Unfortunately, neither the survey nor the 
Budget gives any break-up of the cost between the carrying cost of stocks and 
other costs. 
To reduce this burgeoning foodstocks, the Government of India is 
exporting foodgrains. I am sorry that the international prices of rice and wheat 
are far below our domestic price, since the advanced developed countries 
heavily subsidise the farmers. I just qu ote an instance. The United States of 
America paid its six million farmers a staggering amount of 
286 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
167 billion dollars in 1995-96. So, the Government of India is exporting 
Indian wheat at the price at which it sells it to the BPL consumers. The 
remaining portion, that is fifty per cent of the FCPs so-called 'economic cost', 
is subsidised by the Government and the Government would be spending 
Rs.415 crores--a staggering amount-on each million tonne of wheat exported. 
So is the case with rice. The Government, loath to provide any subsidy to its 
own citizens' consumption, is happy to subsidise export! 
Sir, I must mention this. The height of absurdity has been attained by 
the Antyodaya Anna Yojana launched in  the month of December, 2000, by 
the hon. Prime Minister, on his birth day, no less in true feudal style. This 
scheme is purportedly intended to provide 25 kg. of foodgrains per family per 
month, at a special rate of Rs.2 per kg. for wheat and Rs.3 per kg, for rice. 
However, this is to go only to the poorest of the poor, to 10 million families, 
that is, one-fifth of the Government's so-called estimate or underestimation of 
the poor. How will these lucky 10 million be found out? Have we initiated 
some survey to find out these 10 mill ion families who are the poorest of the 
poor? By what norms will you be dete rmining that? The estimated annual 
allocation of foodgrains for the scheme would be three million tonnes. A 
subsidy of Rs.2315 crores is announced by you. This ridiculous scheme 
shows the direction in which the PDS is heading, virtual winding up, with 
only a few demonstrative crumbs and arbitrarily selected poor families. Sir, it 
is difficult to "avoid the conclusion. Sir, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion 
that the problem of excess foodgrains stocks has been deliberately allowed to 
grow to the crisis proportion in order to strengthen the argument that there is 
no shortage of foodgrains, and so, th ere is no reason that the Public 
Distribution System should continue; secondly, the burden of the procurement 
is too great for the Government to bear and so, it must be left to the private 
traders, the multinational corporations and other companies, and you will be 
finding out your own solace and own logic of divesting the entire property to 
the private traders, the big multinationals or the big Indian companies. That is 
why despite Rs. 4,115 crores overrun in the food subsidies, the World Bank 
and the pro-establishment media have not cared to criticise the gross waste. It 
serves their long term purpose, and Sir, I must say that it is high time for all of 
us, not only the Parliamentarians, but also the good citizens of this country, 
that they must ponder over this very serious situation, where the Government 
has become a party to conspire against the poorest of the poor population of 
this country. It is a conspiracy which has been unmasked, it is a policy 
framework which has been intended to conspire against the common people, 
the poor people of 
287

this country, who are in great majority. Sir, I would conclude by saying that 
unless we ponder over this very important matter here, we shall be wasting 
our time, and we cannot afford to waste our time. With these words, I 
conclude. Thank you very much.
